title: The Country That Grew Its Forest Back

pages.text: Mabel spent the holiday on her uncle’s cocoa farm. At the back, behind the cocoa trees, stood a patch of old forest with one huge tree that three people could not circle with their arms. “Why did you never cut it, Uncle?” she asked. Uncle Bernard patted the trunk. “It gives shade, and it holds the soil. And my father told me never to cut the old ones.”
sentences: Mabel spent the holiday on her uncle’s cocoa farm.
At the back, behind the cocoa trees, stood a patch of old forest with one huge tree that three people could not circle with their arms.
“Why did you never cut it, Uncle?” she asked.
Uncle Bernard patted the trunk.
“It gives shade, and it holds the soil.
And my father told me never to cut the old ones.”
pages.alt: A girl stands beside a farmer and a huge old tree at the edge of a cocoa farm.

pages.text: That evening, Mabel read a story from her geography project: Costa Rica, a small country in Central America. “In the 1980s,” she read, “forest covered just over a fifth of the country, because so much had been cleared for farms and cattle. Today more than half of the country is forest.” She looked up. “Uncle, how can a country double its forest?”
sentences: That evening, Mabel read a story from her geography project: Costa Rica, a small country in Central America.
“In the 1980s,” she read, “forest covered just over a fifth of the country, because so much had been cleared for farms and cattle.
Today more than half of the country is forest.” She looked up.
“Uncle, how can a country double its forest?”
pages.alt: A girl reads from a notebook by lamplight with a map of a small country beside her.

pages.text: Together they read on. Costa Rica passed a law in 1996 that banned turning forest land into farmland. It also started a scheme called payments for ecosystem services, which paid landowners to protect forest, because forests clean water, store carbon and shelter wildlife. “Nearly a million hectares have been in the scheme at some point,” Mabel read. Uncle Bernard whistled. “So the country paid people to keep trees standing,” he said. “That is a new idea to me.”
sentences: Together they read on.
Costa Rica passed a law in 1996 that banned turning forest land into farmland.
It also started a scheme called payments for ecosystem services, which paid landowners to protect forest, because forests clean water, store carbon and shelter wildlife.
“Nearly a million hectares have been in the scheme at some point,” Mabel read.
Uncle Bernard whistled.
“So the country paid people to keep trees standing,” he said.
“That is a new idea to me.”
pages.alt: A farmer and a girl read about a payment scheme with a drawing of coins beside a tree.

pages.text: But Mabel’s article also gave the other side. “The payments have lost more than half their value over time because they were not raised with prices,” she read. “Some experts say the scheme works about as well as national parks, and others say it has not made a big difference. Large landowners can win contracts more easily than small ones, and the forest authority does not always have enough staff to stop illegal cutting.” Uncle Bernard nodded slowly. “Nothing is perfect,” he said.

Large landowners can win contracts more easily than small ones, and the forest authority does not always have enough staff to stop illegal cutting.” Uncle Bernard nodded slowly.
“Nothing is perfect,” he said.
pages.alt: A girl and a farmer study a page with a balance scale showing benefits and problems.

pages.text: “So what would work in Ghana?” asked Mabel. Uncle Bernard counted on his fingers. “We have a Forestry Commission and forest reserves already. But the reserves are being cut by illegal loggers, miners and fire. Reports differ on the main cause: some blame cocoa expansion, others say logging, mining and farming of other crops. The truth is probably all of them.” He smiled wryly. “And farmers like me need to earn something from keeping trees.”

pages.alt: A farmer counts reasons on his fingers beside a map of forest reserves with some marked in red.

pages.text: Back at school, Mabel’s teacher asked each student to argue one side. Mabel chose to argue for paying farmers to keep forest. A classmate argued against, saying that the money should go to schools. “Both of you are making good points,” said the teacher. “A good argument gives a reason, supports it, admits the other side, and ends with a clear conclusion.” Mabel took a deep breath and began to write.
sentences: Back at school, Mabel’s teacher asked each student to argue one side.
Mabel chose to argue for paying farmers to keep forest.
A classmate argued against, saying that the money should go to schools.
“Both of you are making good points,” said the teacher.
“A good argument gives a reason, supports it, admits the other side, and ends with a clear conclusion.” Mabel took a deep breath and began to write.
pages.alt: Two students stand at the front of a class holding notes while a teacher listens.

pages.text: Mabel wrote: “Ghana should reward farmers who protect forest. Firstly, standing forest cleans our rivers and shelters animals that no money can replace. Secondly, Costa Rica shows that payments, together with strong laws, helped its forest to grow back. However, the payments must be fair to small farmers and must keep their value over time. Therefore, I believe the benefits outweigh the cost, provided that the scheme is honest and well managed.”

Secondly, Costa Rica shows that payments, together with strong laws, helped its forest to grow back.
However, the payments must be fair to small farmers and must keep their value over time.
Therefore, I believe the benefits outweigh the cost, provided that the scheme is honest and well managed.”
pages.alt: A girl writes an argument at her desk with a green tree sketched beside the page.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: an argumentative paragraph states an opinion, gives reasons with linking words such as “firstly”, “secondly”, “however” and “therefore”, admits one fair objection and ends with a conclusion. Mabel used full words, no contractions and the same tense throughout. Notice that she did not claim Costa Rica’s system is perfect; honesty makes an argument stronger. The end.

activities.question: What two main things did Costa Rica do?
options: Banned turning forest into farmland and paid landowners to protect forest
Cut more forest and sold timber

Units of land area; one hectare is about the size of a football pitch and a half.
An element stored in trees and soil; too much carbon dioxide in the air warms the planet.
